title: Ecclesiastes 6:1–12
context: Ecclesiastes 6 continues from 5:18–20, where enjoyment is God’s gift, by describing a man who has wealth, honor, children, and long life, yet is not given power to enjoy them. The Preacher’s stark comparison with a stillborn child underlines that abundance without satisfaction is empty. The chapter ends with questions about what is good for man in his brief life and what comes after him. Both traditions read the unit as shared ground about the limits of possessions and of human knowledge.

verses.text: There is an evil which I have seen under the sun, and it is heavy on men:
verses.arminianNotes:
The Preacher names an evil he has seen under the sun that weighs heavily on people. A new observation begins.

Arminian readers see honest attention to life’s burdens rather than easy answers.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse introduces the case that follows and continues the contrast with 5:19, where enjoyment is God’s gift.

Reformed readers see the Preacher facing hard realities within God’s world. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the honesty of biblical wisdom.

verses.text: a man to whom God gives riches, wealth, and honor, so that he lacks nothing for his soul of all that he desires, yet God gives him no power to eat of it, but an alien eats it. This is vanity, and it is an evil disease.
verses.arminianNotes:
God gives a man riches, wealth, and honor so he lacks nothing, yet does not give him power to enjoy them, and a stranger enjoys them instead. This is vanity and a grievous ill.

Arminian readers see the limits of possessions.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse sets God’s giving and withholding side by side without explaining why; Proverbs 16:9 treats how divine direction and human planning relate.

Reformed readers see God’s sovereignty over enjoyment itself. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: If a man fathers a hundred children, and lives many years, so that the days of his years are many, but his soul is not filled with good, and moreover he has no burial, I say that a stillborn child is better than he;
verses.arminianNotes:
If a man has a hundred children and many years, but is not satisfied with good and has no burial, a stillborn child is better off. The comparison is stark.

Arminian readers see that length of life without good is empty.
verses.reformedNotes:
The Preacher’s comparison is deliberately shocking. It underlines that quantity of life is not the same as its fulfillment.

Reformed readers see the emptiness of life without God’s gift of contentment. Both traditions read this soberly as shared ground.

verses.text: for it comes in vanity, and departs in darkness, and its name is covered with darkness.
verses.arminianNotes:
The stillborn comes in vanity, departs in darkness, and its name is covered in darkness. Its life is unseen.

Arminian readers read the image soberly, as part of the Preacher’s argument about the emptiness of an unsatisfied life.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse describes the stillborn as unknown to the world. The Preacher speaks of observable life under the sun, not of eternal destiny.

Reformed readers likewise avoid pressing the image beyond the argument. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: Moreover it has not seen the sun nor known it. This has rest rather than the other.
verses.arminianNotes:
It has not seen or known the sun, yet it has more rest than the other. The comparison concludes.

Arminian readers see the Preacher stressing how heavy an unsatisfied life can be, without making a doctrinal claim about the child.
verses.reformedNotes:
The point concerns rest from the burdens the man carries, not a judgment on the value of the child’s life.

Reformed readers see the image serving the argument. Both traditions read this soberly as shared ground and handle the comparison with care.

verses.text: Yes, though he live a thousand years twice told, and yet fails to enjoy good, don’t all go to one place?
verses.arminianNotes:
Even if he lives two thousand years without enjoying good, do not all go to one place? Death levels all.

Arminian readers see the futility of long life without the enjoyment God gives as a gift to be received with thanks.
verses.reformedNotes:
The phrase ‘one place’ refers to the common end of death, a recurring theme in the book.

Reformed readers see mortality humbling human hopes. Both traditions read this as shared ground and do not use the verse to settle questions about the afterlife.

verses.text: All the labor of man is for his mouth, and yet the appetite is not filled.
verses.arminianNotes:
All human labor is for the mouth, yet the appetite is never filled. Need returns.

Arminian readers see the restless cycle of human desire, which no amount of labor finally satisfies on its own.
verses.reformedNotes:
Appetite here may point beyond physical hunger to deeper longings, though the context concerns desire generally.

Reformed readers see a hunger only God can satisfy. Both traditions read this as shared ground about restless human longing.

verses.text: For what advantage has the wise more than the fool? What has the poor man, that knows how to walk before the living?
verses.arminianNotes:
What advantage has the wise over the fool, or the poor man who knows how to conduct himself before others? The questions press.

Arminian readers see the Preacher testing the limits of wisdom’s benefits.
verses.reformedNotes:
The second question is difficult, and its exact sense is debated.

Reformed readers see wisdom’s value relativized by mortality, though not denied. Both traditions read this as shared ground and hold the meaning of the second question tentatively.

verses.text: Better is the sight of the eyes than the wandering of the desire. This also is vanity and a chasing after wind.
verses.arminianNotes:
Better what the eyes see than the wandering of desire; this also is vanity and chasing wind. Present gifts are better than restless craving.

Arminian readers see contentment as wiser than endless longing.
verses.reformedNotes:
The saying commends enjoying what is at hand over chasing what is absent.

Reformed readers see contentment received from God. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the vanity of restless desire, consistent with the Preacher’s counsel to enjoy one’s portion.

verses.text: Whatever has been, its name was given long ago; and it is known what man is; neither can he contend with him who is mightier than he.
verses.arminianNotes:
Whatever exists was named long ago, and what man is is known; he cannot dispute with one stronger than he. Human limits are fixed.

Arminian readers see humility before realities set beyond human control.
verses.reformedNotes:
The phrase ‘him who is mightier’ is often taken to mean God, though the text does not name him.

Reformed readers see God’s sovereign ordering of all things. Both traditions read this as shared ground, and Proverbs 16:9 treats the related question.

verses.text: For there are many words that create vanity. What does that profit man?
verses.arminianNotes:
Many words increase vanity; what profit is there in them for man? Talk does not change reality.

Arminian readers see a warning against endless argument with what cannot be changed.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse connects with the earlier call to let words be few (5:2).

Reformed readers see humility in speech before God’s ordering of life. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the limits of human argument and the wisdom of restraint.

verses.text: For who knows what is good for man in life, all the days of his vain life which he spends like a shadow? For who can tell a man what will be after him under the sun?
verses.arminianNotes:
Who knows what is good for man in his brief, shadowlike life, and who can tell him what will come after him under the sun? The unit ends with questions.

Arminian readers see human ignorance driving dependence on God.
verses.reformedNotes:
The questions bridge to the sayings of chapter 7, which offer partial answers about what is ‘better.’

Reformed readers see the limits of human knowledge pointing to God alone. Both traditions read this as shared ground.
